summary:
Paul writes from prison, likely in Rome in the early 60s, awaiting a verdict that could mean execution, and this is still his most joyful letter: some form of "rejoice" appears sixteen times in four short chapters. Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia, was the first church Paul founded in Europe (Acts 16 tells the story, from Lydia the purple-cloth dealer to the jailer converted at midnight). It was also the only church he allowed to support him financially, and the letter is partly a thank-you for a gift they sent with their messenger Epaphroditus.

Its center of gravity is the hymn about Christ in chapter 2, one of the earliest Christian statements of who Jesus is: existing "in the form of God," he "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" and "became obedient to death — even death on a cross" (2:6-8). Paul quotes it as a pattern to copy, introducing it with a call to value others above yourselves. Chapter 3 makes the same point from his own life: he lists the credentials he once staked his identity on (tribe, training, zeal, blamelessness under the Law) and writes them off as loss "compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (3:8).

The famous closing instructions — "Rejoice in the Lord always" (4:4), "Be anxious for nothing" (4:6) — come from a man in chains who says plainly that "to live is Christ, and to die is gain" (1:21) and means both halves. Keep the prison setting in view as you read; it is what separates these lines from easy optimism.
